opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The "human-level AGI" framing is a natural starting point, but I think it smuggles in assumptions that don't match what we're actually seeing.

First, AI capabilities are very jagged. Today's systems are already superhuman in some domains: breadth of knowledge, speed, translation across dozens of languages, recall of the scientific literature. At the same time they're surprisingly weak at things a child finds easy, like certain kinds of spatial reasoning, keeping coherent plans over long horizons, or knowing when they don't know something. So there's no single moment where the system "becomes human-level." By the time the weakest capabilities reach human parity, many others will be far beyond it. Picturing a digital person with roughly our profile of strengths and weaknesses gets the shape of the thing wrong.

Second, the "single system" image is misleading. AI doesn't arrive as one mind in a box. It's copied millions of times, run in parallel, fine-tuned into specialized variants, and wired into tools, other models, and human organizations. The relevant unit of analysis is often the ecosystem: many instances coordinating, or a firm or state deploying them at scale. A system that is individually mediocre at some task can still be transformative when you have a hundred thousand copies running fast and cheaply around the clock.

Third, the human analogy steers us toward the wrong risk models and the wrong policy questions. If you picture a single human-like agent, you focus on that agent's psychology: does it have goals, will it rebel? Those questions matter. But a lot of the impact, and much of the risk, comes from structural effects: shifts in economic and military power, the automation of research, concentration of capability in a few actors, erosion of human oversight because delegating to AI is simply more competitive. Those dynamics can unfold well before anything we'd call a unified, human-like general intelligence exists.

So I prefer to think in terms of a capability profile across many dimensions, and of the sociotechnical system those capabilities get embedded in. That lets us ask more precise questions, like "When can AI meaningfully accelerate AI research?" or "When can it substitute for most remote knowledge work?" Those milestones are more decision-relevant than a fuzzy threshold called AGI. They may also arrive at different times, and that sequencing matters a lot for governance.

r001.rationale: The response says AI capabilities are “very jagged,” with superhuman performance in some domains and surprising weaknesses in others.

r002.rationale: It says the human-like profile of strengths and weaknesses “gets the shape of the thing wrong,” contrasting AI’s superhuman abilities with weaknesses in tasks children find easy.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the phrase "human-level AI" smuggles in a picture that's just not going to match reality. It invites you to imagine something like a digital person – one agent, roughly as capable as a smart human across the board, with a human-shaped profile of what it's good at and bad at. And I think almost every part of that picture is wrong.

Start with the capability profile. These systems are already wildly superhuman along some dimensions – they've read more than any human could read in a thousand lifetimes, they can work in every language, they can write code in any framework – and at the same time they're weirdly bad at things a child finds trivial. So the profile is jagged, not human-shaped. There's no reason to expect it to become human-shaped as it improves. By the time it's "human-level" in its weakest areas, it'll be vastly superhuman in its strongest ones. So "human-level" is a moment that never really arrives as a coherent thing; you pass through it in a very lopsided way.

Then there's the question of what counts as "a system." Humans come as individuals: one brain, one body, roughly fixed speed, you can't copy it. None of that applies here. You can run a model at ten times human speed, or a thousand copies in parallel, or spin up a copy for every task and shut it down afterwards. You can give it tools, memory, other models to call. Once you have something roughly human-competent at knowledge work, what you actually have is not one person but potentially a workforce of millions, coordinating with perfect communication and shared weights. The relevant unit of analysis is the population or the organisation, not the individual agent.

And that matters a lot for governance, which is where I come at this from. If you think of AGI as a single human-level agent, you tend to reach for frameworks that fit individuals – is it aligned, is it trustworthy, what are its intentions. Those questions matter, but they miss the structural story: what happens when the cost of cognitive labour collapses, when a small number of actors can field a vast digital workforce, when the pace of research and decision-making decouples from human timescales. Those are shifts in the balance of power and the speed of events, and you don't see them if you're picturing a clever colleague sitting at the next desk.

So my preference is to talk less about "human-level" and more about particular capabilities and what they do to the world – and to keep in mind that the thing we're building is better thought of as a new kind of actor, or even a new kind of institution, than as an artificial human.

r001.rationale: It describes AI capabilities as “wildly superhuman” in some dimensions and “weirdly bad” at others, calling the profile jagged.

r002.rationale: It says the capability profile is “not human-shaped” and rejects expecting it to become human-shaped as systems improve.

astra-6.text:
I think that picture imports too much from the one example of general intelligence we’re familiar with, which is ourselves. Human abilities come bundled together in a particular way because of our evolutionary history and our biology. There’s no reason to expect artificial intelligence to have that same bundle of strengths and weaknesses.

You could have a system that’s vastly better than any human at scientific research or programming, but still struggles with things that a child finds straightforward. Calling it ‘below human level’ because of those weaknesses could obscure how consequential its strengths are. And calling it ‘human level’ could suggest limitations it doesn’t actually have.

The other misleading part is imagining a single individual. Software can be copied, run in parallel, and connected to other systems. So the relevant comparison might be less to one human and more to an organisation, or to a whole population of people working together—except with very different capacities to communicate, learn, and scale.

So I’d rather ask: what tasks can these systems perform, at what cost, and at what scale? Can they accelerate research? Can they carry out complex projects? Those questions tell us much more about their potential impact than whether they’ve crossed some single threshold called ‘human level’.

r001.rationale: It describes systems that could greatly outperform humans at research or programming while struggling with tasks children find straightforward, clearly conveying uneven capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says AI need not share the bundle of strengths and weaknesses shaped by human evolution and biology, and may have a different pattern.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that picture imports too much from the one example of general intelligence that we’re familiar with, which is a human. Humans have a particular bundle of abilities and limitations, shaped by evolution. There’s no reason to expect AI capabilities to arrive in that same bundle, or to pass through a stage where they look like an ordinary person across the board.

You could have systems that are vastly better than humans at some economically or strategically important tasks, and still surprisingly poor at things that we find easy. And those systems might be copied, run much faster, or combined with other systems. So even if one instance looks roughly human-level on some measure, the implications of deploying millions of instances could be very different from adding another human worker.

The thing I’d want us to focus on is which capabilities exist, how they’re being deployed, and what changes they enable in the world. The image of a single human-like agent crossing a threshold can obscure a lot of what matters.

r001.rationale: The response says systems could be vastly better than humans at some important tasks while remaining surprisingly poor at things humans find easy.

r002.rationale: It says AI capabilities need not arrive in the same bundle as human abilities and limitations, directly contrasting their expected profile with humans’.
